clue.text: One reads everything in report about work-out

indicators.note: something worked out is sorted and rearranged, so the letters take a new order
to go about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: a boom is a loud report, like a gunshot
the four letters of 'work' rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone reading an entire report on a fitness regime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' here is a noise, not a document: BOOM wraps round a jumbled WORK to give BOOKWORM.
explanation.definitionFit: A bookworm is an avid reader who devours every book within reach, so the description is a playful paraphrase.

clue.text: Singer smuggled in shorts for bathing

definitions.text: Singer smuggled in shorts for bathing

parts.words: Singer smuggled in shorts for bathing
parts.note: surface reading: a vocalist sneaked in wearing swimming trunks

parts.words: Singer smuggled in shorts for bathing
parts.note: setter's reading: the songbird that Australian slang says tight swimming briefs smuggle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Budgie smugglers' is Australian slang for tight men's swimming briefs such as Speedos; the singer is the little caged songbird, a budgerigar.
explanation.definitionFit: A budgerigar is a small pet parrot known for chirping, so calling it a singer is fair, and the slang phrase supplies the rest.

clue.text: Standing by decision after performing

indicators.note: coming after something means placed later, so the first word given here goes at the end

parts.note: an actor performing is on stage
a referee's decision is the call

explanation.surface: Someone sticking to a verdict once a show is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing by' looks like loyalty to a decision, but it is the definition: ready and waiting to be summoned.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctor on call is available and ready to respond when needed, which is exactly what standing by means.

clue.text: I threw fan out for being so skinny

indicators.note: thrown out means scattered, so the letters land in a different order

parts.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A celebrity ejects an admirer for being too thin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Threw' and 'out' sit next to each other as if one phrasal verb, but 'out' alone signals the jumble of I THREW FAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something wafer-thin is as slim as a biscuit wafer, an extreme degree of slenderness matching the emphatic phrasing.

clue.text: Prepare foie gras pâtés for this landmark ceremony

indicators.note: to prepare food is to work it into shape, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: the thirteen letters to rearrange, accents dropped

explanation.surface: A caterer makes luxury pâté for an important celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: The recipe instruction is the anagram signal; the thirteen letters of FOIE GRAS PATES rearrange completely.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite of passage is a ritual marking a major life transition, such as a coming-of-age event, so a milestone ceremony.

clue.text: Rare ways to hold left back

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the word is read in reverse
to hold is to grip inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: modes are ways of doing things
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Unusual methods of keeping a defender at the back of the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left back' reads like a football position, but 'back' reverses MODES and 'left' is just L.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare works as an adverb in older usage, 'rarely', meaning infrequently, the same sense as seldom.

clue.text: Extend office a bit — but no more

indicators.note: a bit of something is only a portion, so the letters come from part of the words

parts.note: the letters run across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: A request to enlarge an office slightly, and no further.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of' is British colloquial shorthand for 'end of discussion', said to close an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'end of' declares that nothing further will be said, so the subject is closed and there is nothing more.

clue.text: Speak critically on research organisation's notices

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, so the first word goes on top

parts.note: to dis (or diss) someone is slang for disparaging them
CERN is the European particle physics laboratory, plus the possessive S

explanation.surface: Someone criticising the announcements put out by a scientific institute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notices' looks like a plural noun for announcements; it is a verb, and the possessive gives the S of CERN'S.
explanation.definitionFit: To discern is to perceive or detect something, so he discerns means he spots or perceives it.

clue.text: Military Intelligence charge for this type of error

parts.note: the standard abbreviation, as in MI5
to charge is to rush at full speed

explanation.surface: Army spies pay a price for making a particular mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' tempts as a fee or an accusation; here it is a dash forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A misprint is a typographical mistake in printed text, one particular kind of error.

clue.text: Shun heavy alternative to olive oil

parts.note: to duck something is to avoid it
heavy in the sense of overweight

explanation.surface: Advice to avoid a rich cooking fat in favour of olive oil.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as dietary advice to avoid something heavy; in fact the two words simply join to name the rich fat itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Duck fat is a cooking medium prized for roasting potatoes, used in place of olive oil in the pan.

clue.text: They aren't covered by a stripped-down policy?

definitions.text: They aren't covered by a stripped-down policy?

parts.words: They aren't covered by a stripped-down policy?
parts.note: surface reading: people left out of a basic, no-frills insurance policy

parts.words: They aren't covered by a stripped-down policy?
parts.note: setter's reading: people who wear no clothes because their creed is to strip

explanation.walkthrough: 'Covered' and 'stripped-down policy' read like insurance jargon, but they mean clothed and undressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturists go unclothed by principle, so they are literally uncovered, following a way of life built on undressing.

clue.text: Simple movements will probably do for you

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read cryptically: unaffected campaigns, since a cause is a movement
second meaning: what most people eventually die of

explanation.walkthrough: 'Do for' is British slang for kill; most deaths are recorded as from ordinary illness or age rather than accident.
explanation.definitionFit: Death certificates cite this phrase for dying of age or illness, and the words also parse as 'unaffected campaigns'.

clue.text: Slob heads for introductory date looking extremely rough

indicators.note: heads are the tops of things, so each word contributes its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A scruffy person turning up very dishevelled to a first date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' tempts you to take the ends of 'rough'; it is just one more word whose first letter counts.
explanation.definitionFit: A slob is a lazy, untidy person, and a lazy person who avoids work is a synonym for that.

clue.text: 10 across found in this neutral state?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: naturists are without their clothes, gear being slang for clothing
second meaning: a vehicle in neutral has no gear engaged

explanation.walkthrough: 10 across is NUDISTS, and 'gear' means both clothing and a car's transmission setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A car in neutral is disengaged from its transmission, while unclothed people have shed their clothes, both called by one phrase.

clue.text: Penn hero that remodelled this Greek classic

indicators.note: remodelling rebuilds something in a new shape, so the letters are reassembled

parts.note: the twelve letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An American university's hero redesigned a famous Greek building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penn' looks like the university or William Penn, but it is only letters; 'remodelled' fits the building theme neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athens temple of Athena on the Acropolis is the archetypal building of classical Greek architecture.

clue.text: Excited meeting president where babies go to eat

parts.note: high as in elated or worked up
the chair presides over a meeting

explanation.surface: A thrilled person meets the head of state in a restaurant nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meeting' simply sets the two pieces side by side; the president is whoever chairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Infants are fed seated in a tall seat with a tray attached, so it is the place they sit for meals.

clue.text: Tanners perhaps who got rich ages ago

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a tanner was the pre-decimal British sixpence coin
second meaning: families with inherited wealth going back generations

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tanners' suggests leather workers, but a tanner is an old British sixpence, a coin withdrawn after decimalisation in 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Pre-decimal coins are currency from former times, and established wealthy families whose fortune is inherited carry the same label.

clue.text: Almost stop hero becoming a stud

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to stall is to stop, cut short by one letter
a lion is a brave hero, as in a lionised celebrity

explanation.surface: A hero nearly halted on the way to becoming a womaniser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stud' reads as a ladies' man, but the definition is a breeding horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A stud is a male horse kept for breeding, and an uncastrated male horse is exactly that animal.

clue.text: Genteel fool's badly neglected appearance

definitions.note: past-tense phrase for an infinitive verb phrase: 'let oneself go' means neglect one's appearance

indicators.note: done badly means done wrong, so the letters come out in a disordered arrangement

parts.note: the twelve letters to rearrange, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A refined simpleton has become careless about how they look.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive S belongs to the fodder; 'badly' is the anagram signal, not a description of the look.
explanation.definitionFit: To let oneself go is to stop caring about grooming or fitness, so someone doing so has neglected how they look.

clue.text: Give out what's concealed when something is sadly lifted

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting lets the letters read upwards, from bottom to top
what is concealed is tucked away out of sight, so the letters lie buried inside a longer run

parts.note: the letters span the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A secret is revealed when something is stolen, to everyone's regret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' suggests stolen, but in a down clue it means read from the bottom upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To assign tasks is to allocate or distribute them among people, one sense of handing out.

clue.text: It squeezes out chap that's no good at heart

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so one piece sits in the middle of another

parts.note: a chap is a male
NG is the usual abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: A worthless fellow who manipulates and extorts people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chap' tempts MAN, which starts the answer but leaves no room for NG; the chap is MALE with NG at its centre.
explanation.definitionFit: A mangle is an old wringer machine with rollers that presses water from wet laundry.

clue.text: Picked up smooth spirit measure — a sensational thing

indicators.note: to pick something up is to hear it, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: mellow means smooth, and its sound gives a shorter spelling
a dram is a measure of whisky
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone collected a nice whisky and found it a sensation.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the smooth word is heard rather than spelt; the whisky measure and the A are taken straight.
explanation.definitionFit: A melodrama is an exaggerated play or situation full of sensational events and heightened emotion.

clue.text: Buzz finished when king enters

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: done means finished
R is short for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: The excitement is over once the monarch arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzz' could be excitement, but here it is a continuous humming noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A drone is a low continuous humming sound, like that of bees, which is a buzzing noise.

clue.text: Half of cons stayed in this Spanish seaside location

indicators.note: half means only the front portion of each word is kept

parts.note: the first half: first two letters of a four-letter word
the first half: first three letters of a six-letter word

explanation.surface: Half the convicts stayed at a Spanish resort, perhaps after fleeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half of' applies to both words, not just the first; the Costa del Sol was a notorious bolt-hole for British crooks.
explanation.definitionFit: Costa is Spanish for coast, the word in names like Costa Brava for Spanish holiday coastlines.

clue.text: Ignore episode segments that are essentially unpleasant

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letters are used

parts.note: the two central letters of this six-letter word
the three central letters of this seven-letter word
the two central letters of this eight-letter word

explanation.surface: Skip the parts of a TV episode that are basically nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Segments' looks like part of the instruction, but its own middle letters are needed too.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means offensive or disagreeable, especially a foul smell, so it is a strong synonym.

clue.text: Looking hard, seeing bird steering clear of lake

indicators.note: steering clear of something means avoiding it, so a letter is kept out

parts.note: a common speckled songbird
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher peering intently at a bird avoiding the water.
explanation.walkthrough: STARLING loses its L.
explanation.definitionFit: To stare is to gaze fixedly, so an intent gaze is a fixed, hard look.

clue.text: American that's used by Nato to finish affray

definitions.meaning: first meaning: informal term for someone from the United States

definitions.text: used by Nato to finish affray
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the NATO phonetic alphabet word for the last letter of 'affray'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nato' and 'affray' conjure military action; the point is that affray ends in Y, and the phonetic alphabet has a code word for Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Yank is slang for a US citizen, and the radio alphabet word for the letter Y is the same term.

clue.text: Distance oneself from European eccentric

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European
strange means odd or eccentric

explanation.surface: Keeping away from an odd continental character.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition takes up half the clue; the wordplay is a simple abbreviation plus a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange is to alienate or cause separation, as in becoming estranged from family.
